extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, policymakers and journalists interested in U.S. law, remote sensing, and satellite imagery policy
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the Kyl–Bingaman Amendment (P.L. 104-201, §1064), its prohibitions on licensing high-resolution satellite imagery of Israel, the NOAA/ACCRES review process for image-resolution limits, and the law's impacts on visibility, research, and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kyl–Bingaman Amendment prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kyl–Bingaman Amendment (Public Law 104-201, Section 1064) "prohibits US authorities from granting a license for collecting or disseminating high resolution satellite imagery of Israel at a higher resolution than is available from other commercial sources, that is, from companies outside of the United States."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory prohibition is implemented in practice by U.S. regulatory review (NOAA/ACCRES). The article emphasises that the law effectively restricts American commercial providers (e.g., Maxar, Google, Bing) from offering higher-resolution imagery of Israel than available from foreign commercial sources, and has been described as unique U.S. government censorship of commercial satellite images for Israel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to the prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit exception: licensing/collection/dissemination may be allowed if done by a U.S. federal agency, or if done "in order to abolish the secrecy of such recordings."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amendment contains these carve-outs; they are the only exceptions mentioned on the page. Practical implementation depends on agency determinations and regulatory processes (NOAA/ACCRES).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image resolution limit (Ground Sampling Distance) as the operative metric
rubrics_metrics.description: NOAA/ACCRES historically enforced a 2 meter Ground Sampling Distance (GSD) limit for imagery of Israel; in July 2020 NOAA revised the effective limit to 0.4 m GSD based on findings about foreign commercial availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeline and evidence in the article: ACCRES announced a review in Aug 2017; research by Zerbini & Fradley (2018) showed sub-2m imagery available from Airbus and others since 2012; NOAA initially rejected that evidence in Oct 2018 but after further review (2019) published a Federal Register decision (21 July 2020) dropping the GSD limit to 0.4 m, finding twelve companies in eight countries offering imagery superior to 2 m and that 0.4 m products of Israel were readily available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial-availability test for permissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether higher-resolution imagery may be licensed or disseminated by U.S. actors is determined by whether such imagery is commercially available from non-U.S. sources; NOAA evaluates commercial availability when reviewing the KBA restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes ACCRES/NOAA reviews that examine evidence (companies, satellites, product GSDs, nations offering data) to decide if the commercial-availability criterion is met. It also notes concerns about NOAA's transparency (e.g., inability to publish methodology in an earlier review) and cites the Federal Register finding as the formal basis for the 0.4 m change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic scope of the restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: The KBA's restriction on satellite image collection and dissemination has been extended in practice to include the Palestinian territories and the Golan Heights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states this extension (marked 'citation needed') and explains the practical consequences: reduced visibility of Israeli-controlled territories, including obscuring settlement expansion and demolitions. The geographic scope therefore matters for regulatory determinations and impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported impacts on science and commerce as a policy consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: KBA has hindered scientific research (e.g., climate scientists, archaeologists) that rely on high-quality satellite imagery and has undermined U.S. technology companies' business interests by restricting collection and dissemination of such imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a legal requirement, these documented impacts appear in regulatory debate and reviews (e.g., ACCRES minutes, academic research). Regulators and policymakers may weigh these practical effects when assessing or revising the commercial-availability determination and GSD limits.
